groups.title: Short text: the paperless office
groups.text:
To all staff

As announced at the last staff meeting, the company will move all its paperwork to a digital system from the first of next month. This means that in future we want to stop using printed paper almost completely. The aim is to make our work faster and, at the same time, better for the environment.

What this means for you: from that date, all invoices, holiday requests and sick notes must be sent and processed through our new staff portal, "EasyOffice". We will no longer accept paper forms.

We know that it will take everyone some time to get used to the new system. For this reason, there will be training sessions for every department next week, and all staff must attend one. If you have technical problems or questions about how to use the portal, please email the IT helpdesk (helpdesk@example.co.uk), not the HR department.

Kind regards
The Management Team

questions.prompt: The company wants to use less paper in future.
From next month, how must staff send in sick notes?
options: In person, at the HR office.
On a paper form, as before.

questions.prompt: What should staff do if they have questions about the new system?
options: Send an email to the IT helpdesk.
Ask the manager at the next staff meeting.
Cancel their place on the training.
questions.answer: Send an email to the IT helpdesk.

groups.title: B1 reading, task 1: match the adverts to the people
groups.text:
a) Online English for beginners (A1–A2), mornings – Monday to Friday, 9.00–11.00 am, by video call. For learners with no English at all. £3 per lesson.
b) Evening English B1 (online) – Tuesdays and Thursdays, 6.30–8.30 pm. Only for learners who have finished an A2 course. Free for people in paid work. You need a laptop or computer.
c) English for parents, with a crèche (in person) – Monday to Wednesday, 9.30 am–12.30 pm, at the Westbridge Family Centre. Free childcare for children aged 1 and over.
d) Flexible online course with recorded lessons (B1–B2) – Watch every lesson as a video, whenever you like. Live group session on Saturdays at 10 am. Ideal if your working hours change. £15 a month.
e) Reading and writing from the start (online, tablet loan) – For adults who first want to learn to read and write. Monday, Wednesday and Friday, 9–11 am. Borrow a tablet for free.
f) Intensive online course B2–C1 – Monday to Friday, 1–4.30 pm, for five weeks. You must have a B1 certificate. £180 (you can pay in instalments).

Example: A person is looking for a course only at the weekend, because they work during the week. → d

groups.title: B1 reading, task 2: newspaper article – true or false?
groups.text:
More and more adult classes move online

For some years now, many colleges and adult learning centres have offered their courses online as well as in the classroom. For people with children, people who work shifts and people who live a long way from the nearest college, this makes life much easier. At Westbridge Adult Learning, a group of ten learners is currently studying together by video call, among them Aylin Demir, Vera Salieva and Kofi Mensah. "At first the technology was new to me," says Aylin Demir, "but after two weeks I could use the video app as easily as my phone." Their teacher, Ms Keller, explains that online lessons work differently from the classroom, especially for speaking practice: "We do a lot of work in small groups, in what we call breakout rooms. That way everybody speaks more, not just the loudest people." Some learners say that their internet connection is sometimes slow, but on the whole most of them are happy: almost all of them want to take their next course online too.

questions.prompt: Many colleges now offer online courses.
Aylin Demir found the video app easy to use from the first day.
In breakout rooms, learners work in small groups.
All the learners have a fast, reliable internet connection.
Most of the learners want to do their next course online.

groups.title: B1 reading, task 3: forum posts – who says this?
groups.text:
Marek Nowak: "I think online lessons are great, because I don't have to travel across town after work. I save more than an hour every day."
Priya Sharma: "I sometimes find it harder to concentrate online. I miss being in the same room as the other learners."
Yasmin Haddad: "At first I was scared of speaking in front of the camera. Now I actually put my hand up more often than I did in the classroom."
Lin Wei: "I like being able to watch the recordings again when I haven't understood something. It really helps me when I revise."

questions.prompt: This person saves time by learning online.
This person sometimes finds it harder to concentrate online than in a classroom.
This person speaks more now than in face-to-face lessons.
This person uses the video recordings to revise.

groups.title: B1 reading, task 4: interview
groups.text:
Question: Dr Fielding, how have your classes changed in recent years?
Answer: A few years ago, almost every course took place in a classroom. Today about half of our courses are also available online. That helps people with small children or people who work shifts in particular.

Question: Are there any disadvantages?
Answer: Yes. Not everyone has a quiet place to study or a reliable internet connection. That's why learners without a computer of their own can borrow a tablet from us.

Question: What advice would you give new learners?
Answer: I'd recommend getting to know the technology before the first lesson and joining the online waiting room on time. And if you have a question, don't be shy about turning your camera on – it makes a huge difference to your speaking.

questions.prompt: According to Dr Fielding, how many courses are now available online?
According to the interview, who do online classes help in particular?
options: only people who speak no English
people with small children or shift work
only people who have lived in the UK for years
questions.answer: people with small children or shift work

questions.prompt: What can learners without a computer get?
options: a place on a classroom course

questions.prompt: What does Dr Fielding advise new learners to do?
options: get to know the technology first
questions.answer: get to know the technology first

writingPrompt.title: Writing: reply to David
writingPrompt.context: Your friend David has sent you an email. He is coming to visit your town next month and has some questions. Write a reply to David.
writingPrompt.email:
Hi!

How are you? I hope everything's going well. I've got some good news: I'm coming to your town for a long weekend next month, from Friday 14th to Monday 17th! I can't wait to see you again.

I've got a few questions. Are you free that weekend? What should we do while I'm there? Is there anything I really have to see? And what's the weather usually like at that time of year – do I need to bring a warm coat?

I'd also love to try some local food, so if you know a good place to eat, let me know.

Write back soon!

Best wishes,
David
points: Say how you feel about David's visit.
Say if you are free that weekend.
Suggest two things you could do together.
Tell him what the weather is usually like and what to bring.
writingPrompt.tips: Write at least 60–80 words · Don't forget a greeting at the start and a sign-off at the end · Write full sentences

errorHunt.title: Error hunt: model text with mistakes
errorHunt.context: Writing task (B1, about 30 minutes): You live in a block of flats. All the tenants are supposed to keep the stairs and hallway clean, but none of your neighbours do it. Write a letter to your landlord, Mr Hughes. The model text below contains mistakes – a teacher's text for proofreading. There is no automatic answer key; this is deliberately an exercise to discuss with a teacher or a study partner.
errorHunt.text:
Flat 4, 27 Mill Lane
Westbridge
12 May 2026

Dear Mr Hughes,

I am writing to you because there is a big problem in our building since two weeks. The stairs and the hallway are very dirty and nobody of my neighbours clean them. I tried to solve the problem by myself. I have spoke with several neighbours and I putted a notice in the hallway. Unfortunately it did not help. The neighbours doesn't care about it.

Also there are other problems in the building. The heating in the basement is not working good, and the light at the entrance is broken. Many residents are afraid when they come home in the evening.

I would like to ask you to take this problem serious and to do something immediately. Please can you speak with all tenants and organise a cleaning rota. The repairs should also be make as soon as possible.

I look forward to hear from you.

Yours faithfully,
Anna Baker
